title: Sinan the architect
hookLine: the architect of a great many buildings, including the Suleymaniye

lines: A MOSQUE AND A SMALL TOWN AROUND IT.
THE SULTAN'S TOMB IN THE GARDEN.
A SMALL TOMB AT THE CORNER.
cards: On a hill above the Golden Horn in Istanbul stands a great mosque with four minarets, and around it, a whole small town: schools, a hospital, a kitchen that fed the poor, a bathhouse, shops.
Behind the mosque, in a garden, lies the tomb of the sultan who paid for it, Suleyman. And just outside the complex, at a street corner, there's another tomb, much smaller, plain and simple.
It belongs to the man who designed all of it. He rests near the sultan he served, but not inside. Today: Sinan the architect.

teach.b: Sinan did not start as an architect. By his own account, given to a friend who wrote it down, he was taken as a young man into the sultan's service and became a soldier.
On campaign, he built bridges and boats for the army. Engineering under pressure, with rivers to cross and no time to waste.
Only later was he made chief architect of the empire, and from then on, mosques, schools, bridges, bathhouses, fountains and kitchens came off his drawing board across the Ottoman lands.
Tradition credits him with a great many buildings. The Suleymaniye, the complex on that hill, was built for Suleyman.

Sinan himself, in his memoirs, sorted three of his mosques like stages in a craftsman's life: an early one in Istanbul as his apprentice work, the Suleymaniye as the work of a journeyman, and the Selimiye in Edirne as his masterpiece.
What was he chasing? Space and light.

teach.h: ONE CARPET UNDER ONE SKY OF LIGHT.
teach.b: Under his great domes, the room opens out so there's little in the way, and windows set high and low let the light fall evenly across the floor.
Muslims gather in rows on one carpet, shoulder to shoulder, facing Mecca, and Sinan's domes give those rows a single, unbroken sky. The Qur'an's verse of light comes to mind in rooms like these.
In Pickthall's translation: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." A dome doesn't explain that verse. But it can make a crowd go quiet.

how: Sinan's mosques, including the Suleymaniye in Istanbul and the Selimiye in Edirne, are still used for daily and Friday prayers, with worshipers in rows under their domes.

games.q: you're Sinan, designing a mosque where crowds will pray in long rows, shoulder to shoulder. what do you want under the dome?
o: many columns, close together, to hold up the roof.
one wide open space, with as little in the way as possible.
a maze of small rooms, one for each group.
games.why: Sinan's domes open the room out, so the rows of worshipers stand together under a single, unbroken sky.

practice: Look up at whatever ceiling is above you, or at a photo of the inside of the Suleymaniye's dome. Notice where the light comes from, and how the shape gathers your eyes upward. If you pray, you can let the looking become prayer.

wordCard.voice: Sinan. The soldier-engineer who became the Ottoman chief architect, designed the Suleymaniye, and filled his domes with light. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a builder, an architect; Sinan is remembered as Mimar Sinan.
